gap: None of the results ChatGPT got say that the large '2000 W' rating on combination travel converters covers heating-only appliances and is limited in time. The Voltage Valet VCSB/VCSP manual limits its 2000 W setting to non-electronic heating appliances, run for at most 10 minutes and then left off for at least 60. It also warns that electronically controlled curling irons and straighteners may be damaged on that setting. US electronics only get the small side: 50 W on the Voltage Valet, 200 W on TESSAN's combo and 250 W on the TESSAN TC03.
standout_why: I opened three rival pages from ChatGPT's results. globalplugs.com/blog/voltage-converter-vs-adapter explains continuous versus surge watts in general terms and names no products. doace.com adapter-vs-converter-vs-transformer says only that 'some converters output a stepped or modified waveform' and has nothing on dual modes or duty cycles. voltwander.com/faq covers sizing only ('1000W+ step-down converter'). None of them separates a converter's heating-mode watts from its electronics-mode watts or gives a time limit. ChatGPT's answer quoted '200W' (Ceptics) and '250W' (Tessan) without saying what those numbers cover. The ace.aaa.com page came back as a title only, and I could not read the TESSAN, FOVAL and Ceptics manual pages or the Digital Camera World review, so I could not check those.
decides: This confirms that a compact all-in-one adapter-converter is a pick for low-watt US electronics only. The TESSAN TC03 is rated 250 W 'maximum', and TESSAN lists phones, tablets, cameras, headphones and small personal electronics as suitable. Combos advertising 2000 W, such as TESSAN's 3-outlet model with 4 USB ports, reach that figure only on a separate heating-appliance side, which TESSAN itself calls a 'peak' rating. On Voltage Valet's equivalent setting the duty cycle is 10 minutes on and 60 off, and electronically controlled styling tools are excluded. So a shopper with a US hair dryer or digital straightener should not treat any of these as a 2000 W converter. A dual-voltage appliance is the safer answer. The page's table should show the electronics-side watts and the heating-side watts as separate columns, with the duty cycle as a footnote.
